title: America's Cyber Agency Is Using Anthropic's AI to Hunt Bugs in Government Code. India's $108 Billion IT Industry Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: CISA's deployment of the Mythos model to scan federal software for vulnerabilities signals a shift that could reshape the government IT services market dominated by Indian outsourcing firms.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • CISA is using Anthropic's AI to scan government software for vulnerabilities.
  • The Indian IT industry, worth $108 billion, may face disruption from AI advancements.
  • Anthropic's AI models are now trusted by US agencies after initial blacklisting.
  • Indian firms like TCS and Infosys are pivoting to AI-augmented services.
  • India seeks access to advanced AI tools for cybersecurity through Project Glasswing.

America's frontline cyber defence agency is using Anthropic's most powerful AI model to hunt for vulnerabilities in government software — a development that underscores both the transformative potential and the political volatility of frontier AI, with direct implications for the Indian IT industry that services billions of dollars in US government contracts.

Three people familiar with the programme told Reuters on Monday that the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is deploying Anthropic's Mythos model to scan government code repositories for bugs that could be exploited by foreign spies and cybercriminals. The audits are being conducted by CISA's Attack Surface Evaluation team, a specialised unit that runs security assessments and penetration tests across federal agencies.

The sources said the scans have already uncovered "a large number" of vulnerabilities, though neither the nature nor the severity of the bugs has been publicly disclosed.

A Turbulent Partnership

The revelation comes against the backdrop of one of the most fraught relationships in Silicon Valley-Washington history. Anthropic, which has confidentially filed for a US initial public offering, was effectively blacklisted by the Pentagon in February after it refused to remove safeguards preventing its AI from being used in autonomous weapons systems or domestic surveillance. The Department of Defence slapped the company with a formal supply-chain risk designation — a label previously reserved for foreign firms suspected of espionage.

> "The sources said the scans have already uncovered "a large number" of vulnerabilities, though neither the nature nor the severity of the bugs has been publicly disclosed."

That standoff has since thawed. The National Security Agency began using Mythos earlier this year, and last week the Commerce Department lifted export controls on Anthropic's most advanced Fable and Mythos models after a three-week global shutdown that left enterprise clients scrambling. A federal judge had already blocked the Pentagon's designation in March.

The whiplash — blacklisted one month, auditing government code the next — captures the uncomfortable reality that the US government simultaneously fears and depends on the same handful of AI companies.

What This Means for Indian IT

The Indian technology services industry earned $108 billion in export revenue last year, with roughly 60 per cent coming from the United States. Companies like TCS, Infosys, and Wipro hold massive contracts to build, maintain, and secure software for US federal agencies, state governments, and defence contractors.

If AI models like Mythos can audit government code at scale — identifying vulnerabilities faster and more cheaply than human teams — the implications for India's IT workforce are significant. The country's outsourcing giants have built two-decade-old business models around deploying large teams of engineers for exactly this kind of work: code reviews, security assessments, compliance testing.

The pivot is already visible. TCS and Infosys have both announced major AI integration strategies this year, positioning themselves as providers of AI-augmented services rather than pure headcount plays. But the transition is uneven, and tens of thousands of mid-level engineers whose daily work involves the kind of pattern-matching that Mythos excels at are watching the landscape shift beneath them.

Impact of AI on Indian IT

›60% of revenue from US contracts

India Wants the Same Tools

The CISA programme connects to a broader India-US technology thread. Just two days ago, reports emerged that New Delhi is seeking access to Anthropic's most powerful AI models through an initiative codenamed Project Glasswing, which would give Indian cybersecurity agencies similar code-auditing capabilities. Washington is reportedly "listening carefully" but has not yet agreed.

The irony is sharp: India wants the same AI tools that America's own agencies are only now learning to trust — and that Washington itself tried to shut down just weeks ago.

Meanwhile, the Commerce Department's decision to lift export controls came in tandem with OpenAI delaying a full public launch of GPT-5.6 at the government's request. Britain's Financial Conduct Authority warned on Monday that regulators globally need to grapple with the growing influence of frontier AI models, noting that more than a quarter of UK consumers already trust tools like ChatGPT and Claude for financial guidance.

CISA's AI Deployment Timeline

Pentagon blacklists Anthropic over AI safeguards.
March 2023
Federal judge blocks Pentagon's designation of Anthropic.
Early 2023
NSA begins using Mythos model.

Commerce Department lifts export controls on Anthropic's models.
Sources: Reuters

For the millions of Indian IT professionals whose livelihoods depend on American technology spending, the message is clear: the age of AI-powered government is arriving, and the business models that built Bangalore's tech corridor are being rewritten in real time.

*Sources: Reuters, CNN, UK Financial Conduct Authority, New York Post*
